sentences.text: Cerrejonisuchus possessed a very short snout that was narrow and kept the same width from the nose to the eyes. The nostrils sat right at the very front of this snout. Its teeth were mostly uniform in shape, but the third upper tooth was larger while the fourth was smaller. Unlike many relatives, these teeth were straight rather than curved.
This animal held the record for being the smallest dyrosaur ever discovered based on body length estimates. It also had the shortest snout of any known member of this group.

The genus Cerrejonisuchus was named by Hastings and colleagues in 2010. The type species is C. improcerus. Fossils were recovered from the Cerrejón open-pit coal mine in La Guajira, Colombia. The only known remains include a holotype skull, lower jaws, a skull with a partial skeleton, and a partial snout. All these specimens come from a specific area below Vein 90 at Mina La Puente.

Scientists believe its short snout helped it eat a wide variety of food including fish, insects, frogs, lizards, small snakes, and perhaps mammals. This adaptation may have allowed it to fill a new ecological role in the tropical rainforests of Paleocene Colombia.

Its flat skull and compressed, uniform teeth suggest it lived on land as a predator. This presence in Colombia indicates that dyrosaurids diversified in South America after the mass extinction at the K–T boundary. It might have even been prey for the giant snake Titanoboa in their shared brackish waters.

A 2010 study placed Cerrejonisuchus near the base of the dyrosaur family tree between Phosphatosaurus and Arambourgisuchus. Although it shares a short snout with Chenanisuchus, the two are not closely related, proving that snout shape does not define family history in dyrosaurs. Along with Anthracosuchus, it is one of the few dyrosaurids with this feature. It belongs to the family Dyrosauridae.

Cerrejonisuchus lived during the Middle to Late Paleocene epoch. The fossils come from sediments formed in a brackish water environment where rivers met lagoons. The age of the Cerrejón Formation is determined by carbon isotopes, pollen, spores, and dinoflagellate cysts. It inhabited this transitional setting from the Selandian to the Thanetian stages, between 61.66 and 56 million years ago.
